title: Can Chevron Build a Lithium Business in the Smackover Formation? - The Globe and Mail
content: Chevron Corporation CVX entered the U.S. lithium sector in June 2025, when it announced two leasehold acquisitions in the Smackover Formation in Northeast Texas and Southwest Arkansas. The company initially put the combined position at about 125,000 net acres and later revised that figure to about 135,000 net acres. Chevron acquired the leases to find out whether it can produce lithium from salty water found deep underground. The company is pursuing lithium mainly for energy storage, including batteries used in electric vehicles and on the power grid. Chevron is assessing the underground resource, testing direct lithium extraction and designing the facilities it would need. The process separates lithium from salty water pumped to the surface, then returns the remaining water to the underground reservoir. That work draws on skills Chevron already uses in its oil and gas business, from assessing reservoirs to drilling wells and handling fluids. The company is also refining its product specifications so it can discuss with potential customers what they need and what the project might eventually be able to supply. Chevron plans to develop the acreage in phases and adjust the pace to market conditions. The company has yet to announce when commercial production might start or how much lithium it aims to produce. Oil and gas production still drives most of Chevron’s earnings, so the near-term question for investors is what the extraction tests reveal about the project’s economics. How much lithium Chevron can recover from the brine, and what it costs to recover it, will help determine whether the acreage can support a profitable business. A U.S. lithium supply chain depends on producers being able to meet battery makers’ quality standards consistently. Producing battery-grade lithium in small batches is an early step. The next test is whether that quality holds as output increases. ExxonMobil Holdings XOM holds brine rights across more than 300,000 net acres in the Smackover Formation. ExxonMobil has produced battery-grade lithium carbonate at its Texas pilot facility using brine from southern Arkansas. ExxonMobil’s preliminary agreement with LG Chem for a potential lithium supply deal is nonbinding. The company aims to produce enough lithium for about one million electric vehicles a year by the first half of the 2030s. Occidental Petroleum OXY is testing direct lithium extraction in California’s Imperial Valley through a joint venture with BHE Renewables. Occidental’s TerraLithium subsidiary and its partner produced battery-grade lithium carbonate from geothermal brine and converted lithium chloride into lithium hydroxide in separate tests. Occidental and its partner expect demonstration operations to continue through 2027 as they assess whether the process is economically viable at commercial scale. Shares of Chevron have gained some 13% in the past six months, contrary to the Oil/Energy sector’s 6% loss. From a valuation perspective — in terms of forward price-to-earnings ratio — Chevron is trading at a premium compared with the industry average. content:
If you only skimmed the headlines about record ExxonMobil profits and political scrutiny of fuel prices, you might expect shareholders to have been whipsawed. The shares cost US$116 at the start of the period, and ExxonMobil sat between two very different stories about what came next. On the optimistic side, one view saw a fair value of US$124, a price implied by assumptions that future dividend strength and global projects in areas like Guyana and the Permian Basin would support higher production volumes and improved margins across cycles. The more cautious script put fair value closer to US$78, built on expectations that reliance on fossil fuels, revenue growth declining 1.0%, and profit margins at 7.9% would leave the business exposed to energy transition and regulatory pressure. The biggest fact to land after November 2025 was ExxonMobil’s Q3 2026 report. Revenue was US$110,503m and net income reached US$15,413m, compared with US$83,331m and US$7,548m a year earlier, while net margin moved from 9.1% to 13.9%. That combination of higher sales and fatter margins clearly leaned toward the optimistic case built on efficiency and project execution, although it did not erase long term transition risks. The clear takeaway is that a thesis built on “better margins from advantaged projects” depends on reported profitability. When testing a similar story elsewhere, track whether net margin and absolute earnings move in the same direction as the promise, then judge the share price separately from those operating results. Price remains below the 7-day SMA at $159.17, the 20-day SMA at $164.55 and the 50-day SMA at $172.47, which keeps the trend structure tilted lower rather than confirming a durable turn. That matters because the current price is sitting only slightly above the pivot point at $158.45 and not far from immediate support at $156.89. In practical terms, XOM is still trading inside a narrow decision zone, where small moves can either build a base or quickly roll back into support. The daily RSI of 33.06 sits in a neutral-to-soft zone, while the MACD reading of -4.0619 with a flat histogram signals momentum that is still depressed rather than improving decisively. Stochastic readings at 13.22 for %K and 10.58 for %D also point to an oversold posture, but oversold does not mean reversal on its own. Bollinger positioning reinforces that point. XOM is near the lower band at $155.07, with %B at 0.1705, which shows price is pressing into the lower part of its recent range. That can invite a bounce, but it also means the market is still priced for caution until buyers can reclaim the middle band at $164.55. Immediate resistance sits at $159.85, followed by stronger resistance at $161.41. Those are the first checkpoints for any recovery attempt. If XOM clears them, the next task would be to reclaim the 20-day average at $164.55, which would improve the quality of the rebound. On the downside, immediate support is $156.89 and strong support is $155.49. With ATR(14) at $4.04, XOM has enough daily volatility to test either side of that band quickly. On Binance perpetual futures, the funding rate is -0.2038%, which means shorts are paying longs. That usually tells you positioning is leaning bearish enough to create pressure for a snapback if price starts lifting, but it does not prove a sustained bullish turn. Open interest adds a more conservative read. XOM open interest fell 22.43% over 24 hours to 3,713.21 contracts, while the daily open interest value is $364,220. That kind of decline is more consistent with position closing and liquidation than fresh commitment. The long/short ratios are only mildly positive for bulls: Binance global accounts are 52.7% long versus 47.3% short, and top traders are 51.9% long versus 48.1% short. At the same time, the 1-hour taker buy/sell ratio of 0.5058, with buy volume at 140 and sell volume at 277, shows aggressive selling pressure is still dominating the tape. Those are supportive signals for the equity story, but they do not override the near-term price structure. title: 'Exxon Got Walloped': $340 Million Legal Blow Paves The Way For More - Investor's Business Daily

BREAKING: Dow Rises, Nasdaq Slashes Losses In Wild Session A district judge recently dealt ExxonMobil (XOM) a $339.56 million blow over oil sludge that's "continuously seeped" into soil, surface water, and an aquifer in northwest Louisiana for half a century. Legal experts say the first-of-its-kind judgment paves the way for future citizen lawsuits against oil giants in the state, which has long rated among the most polluted in the U.S. "Exxon got walloped," said Robert Verchick, a professor of environmental law at Loyola University New Orleans. "I definitely think we will see more lawsuits like this," he said, due to the size of the verdict and the $12.7 million in fees awarded to the attorneys. The 42nd Judicial Court in DeSoto Parish, Louisiana, found that an Exxon predecessor — Standard Oil Company of Louisiana — had, since 1954, abandoned 43 unlined pits of sludge across 243 acres of land. The court identified five violations against the state's Environmental Quality Act — for the pollution itself, for not cleaning it up and for failing to report it. But the daily fines levied against Exxon only stretch back to 1980, when the state enacted the environmental law. The plaintiffs sought $848.9 million, all of which would've gone to the state, according to Verchick. The plaintiffs and legal experts expect the company to appeal. A spokesperson for Exxon said the company doesn't comment on pending litigation. Exxon said it only learned of the pollution through the lawsuit, according to the Oct. 30 judgment. "The court considers the (nearly $340 million) penalty to be large enough that Exxon will not consider it to be merely the cost of doing business and believes it will deter this action in the future," the judgment said. For context, Exxon told investors it had $12.2 billion in cash and cash equivalents on hand at the end of the third quarter (ending Sept. 30). In the quarterly filing, the company called the likelihood that lawsuits brought against it will harm its financial condition "remote." Analysts project that Exxon's coffers will nearly double to $23.2 billion in Q4 and rise to $94.2 billion by the end of the decade, according to a FactSet consensus. "This is the biggest penalty I've ever seen in a citizen suit under state or federal law," said Patrick Parenteau, an emeritus professor and senior climate policy fellow at Vermont Law and Graduate School. In an email, he called the nearly $13 million in additional attorney fees, to be paid by Exxon, a "huge incentive for more cases." Parenteau cited Shell (SHEL), BP (BP), Sunoco (SUN) and Suncor (SU) among other potential near-term targets for environmental suits in the state. In Louisiana, citizens can sue for violations of the state's environmental laws, but they have to give the state a chance to prosecute first. If the state government declines to do so, they effectively get the go-ahead, explained Verchick. Environmental laws have such provisions "because, the idea is, you can't always rely on government enforcers because there's not enough resources," he said. "Because the fines don't go to the citizen," Verchick added, "you are looking at a plaintiff who's just really interested in fairness and in getting this thing cleaned up," rather than seeking a lot of money in a "tort" lawsuit to settle a civil wrong. Parenteau sees cases rising across the U.S. against oil firms for the "legacy pollution they are leaving behind." He called Louisiana "a veritable hotbed for this litigation." In the first quarter, Exxon warned investors that local Louisiana governments have filed "unprecedented legal proceedings" against it, "requesting compensation for the restoration of coastal marsh erosion in the state." Exxon called the basis of the cases "meritless." Get these newsletters delivered to your inbox & more info about our products & services. While the Louisiana verdict centers on pollution, Verchick thinks the blue wave will limit oil companies' ability to successfully lobby for protections against climate lawsuits. Verchick believes such cases to be oil companies' primary concern. Victor Flatt, who teaches environmental law at Case Western Reserve University, doesn't see the midterms changing the course of environmental suits at the federal level, citing President Donald Trump's veto powers. But, he said, "certainly the midterms signaled a 'vibe' shift and perhaps more willingness to pursue legacy pollution in general." Flatt expects that the Louisiana lawsuit in particular "will be changed on appeal and/or settled by the state." This year, Exxon, Chevron (CVX), and other supermajor oil names have made a fortune on high gasoline and diesel prices related to the U.S./Israeli war on Iran and the Russia-Ukraine war. title: Your Exxon Dividend Needs Only About $59 Oil - Trefis
content: Today’s big story: Nvidia Added $954 Billion In A Day. Is Jensen Huang Too Big To Fire? Oil has fallen, and oil stocks have fallen with it. WTI crude, the main U.S. oil price, fell 17.3% from $108.21 on Oct 16 to $89.53 on Nov 17. Exxon Mobil stock fell 14.4% in the month to Monday’s close. Chevron fell 11.6%. So what oil price do their payouts actually need? On each company’s own record since 2015, Exxon’s dividend and share buybacks together need WTI to average about $79 a barrel over a year. Chevron’s need about $80. The dividend alone needs much less. That line is about $59 for Exxon and about $65 for Chevron. Oil’s latest print is 12.9% above Exxon’s full-payout line. It is 11.3% above Chevron’s. On this measure, both payouts are still covered. Our read is that the dividends are the safe part, and the buybacks are what cheaper oil would test. Free cash flow is the cash a company keeps after paying for its wells, plants and other capital spending. In the four quarters to September, oil averaged $78.87 a barrel. That is close to the full-payout lines above, about $79 for Exxon and $80 for Chevron. In those months, Exxon’s free cash flow covered its dividend 2.5 times. Its dividends plus buybacks used 87.9% of free cash flow. Chevron’s payouts used 73.3%. Exxon Mobil’s cash covered its quarterly checks to holders 2.5 times over the past year, even as the stock fell 14.4% in a month. If those checks pay your bills, the falling share price is the part you have to sit through. The Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3 times the S&P 500’s, from 50 companies that have paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row. See what it pays. The table below runs the same test on four large U.S. producers, next to each stock’s fall over the past month. All cash figures cover the four quarters from October 2025 to September 2026. Price changes run from the Oct 23 close to the Nov 23 close, price only. ConocoPhillips is the thinnest of the four. Its payouts used 95.5% of free cash flow. EOG Resources covered its dividend 3.4 times, the widest margin in the group. The Energy Select Sector SPDR fund, which holds many of these names, fell 13.6% over the same month. The wider market did not drive Monday’s selling. The SPDR S&P 500 fund rose 4.7% that day, while Exxon fell 1.9%. We set each company’s free cash flow for every calendar year from 2015 to 2025 against that year’s average WTI price. A straight line fits Exxon’s record closely. Each $1 a barrel was worth about $1 billion of Exxon’s yearly free cash flow. For Chevron, each $1 was worth about $714 million. We then found the yearly oil price at which that cash equals the latest twelve months of payouts. A check on 47 single quarters gives nearly the same lines. It puts Exxon’s full-payout line at $78.34 and Chevron’s at $78.08. Today’s companies did better than the old record predicts. At the past four quarters’ $78.87 oil, the fit expected $37.3 billion of free cash flow from Exxon. Exxon produced $43 billion. The fit expected $23.9 billion from Chevron, and Chevron produced $34.1 billion. So the lines above are, if anything, on the high side. For how large Exxon’s cash is next to its share price, see Should You Buy Exxon Mobil Stock For Its Cash? For the same test on Chevron, see Should You Buy Chevron Stock For Its Cash? The twelve-month average hides when the cash arrived. 82.6% of Exxon’s free cash flow came in the April to September quarters. For Chevron the share was 88.3%. Oil averaged $95.65 and $87.11 in those two quarters. A year earlier, oil averaged $68.17. At that price, Exxon’s dividends plus buybacks were 159.5% of its free cash flow. Chevron’s were 167.4%. The gap had to come from the balance sheet. From 2015 to 2025, Exxon’s cash covered its dividend in 7 of 11 years. It covered the full payout in only 5. Chevron covered its dividend in 7 years and the full payout in 4. Exxon raised its dividend per share 4% on its latest quarterly call. Management said that was its 44th straight year of growth in the dividend per share. Asked about buybacks at $60 oil, Exxon’s chief executive answered on the dividend. “We’re not going to ever cut our dividend,” he said. The buyback is less firm. Exxon plans to keep buybacks at $20 billion in 2027, “assuming reasonable market conditions”. Chevron said it has kept buybacks at a rate of $2.5 billion to $3 billion a quarter and intends to stay in that range. Two smaller producers state their own lines, measured differently from ours: The test is the yearly average, not one day’s print. So far this quarter, WTI has averaged $98.76, well above both lines. If oil instead averaged below about $80 for a year, we think buybacks would be the first thing to shrink. The dividends look safe on this record down to about $59 for Exxon and $65 for Chevron. Our read: the recent fall prices in more risk to the dividends than the cash shows. The buybacks are the part that needs oil to average above about $80. That still leaves a holder’s savings tied to one oil price. If one of these stocks is a big part of what you own, it helps to decide ahead of time how and when you would sell. title: ExxonMobil Holdings (XOM) Stock: Shares Slide 1.62% as Company Unveils $3B Debt Buyback Results - Blockonomi
content: ExxonMobil Holdings (XOM) shares declined 1.62% to $157.40, losing $2.59 as selling pressure erased earlier gains. The stock briefly approached $161.70 before retreating toward intraday lows during the trading session. Meanwhile, ExxonMobil announced results from its $3 billion debt repurchase program involving four outstanding note series. ExxonMobil disclosed the pricing terms and final tender results for debt repurchases conducted through two subsidiaries. Pioneer Natural Resources Company and Exxon Mobil Corporation managed separate cash offers covering their respective outstanding notes. The companies launched the offers on November 16, 2026, with a combined repurchase limit of $3 billion. However, total eligible submissions remained below the maximum amount, allowing both subsidiaries to accept every valid tender. Consequently, neither company needed to reduce accepted amounts through proportional allocations across the four note series. The accepted principal totaled approximately $1.76 billion, covering debt obligations with maturities ranging from 2030 through 2040. The transaction includes two Pioneer note series and two Exxon note series with different interest rates. Pioneer offered to repurchase its 1.900% senior notes due 2030 and 2.150% senior notes due 2031. Exxon targeted its 3.482% notes due 2030 and 4.227% notes due 2040 under separate offers. Pioneer accepted $128.68 million in notes due 2030 and $97.79 million in notes due 2031. The company established consideration of $896.86 and $892.94 per $1,000 principal amount for those respective securities. Both series carried pricing spreads of 22 and 30 basis points above their reference Treasury yields. Exxon accepted approximately $705.41 million of its 3.482% notes maturing in 2030. The company also accepted $832.68 million of its 4.227% notes scheduled to mature in 2040. Their respective repurchase prices reached $957.85 and $872.59 per $1,000 principal amount, excluding accrued interest. The companies calculated these prices using reference Treasury yields and predetermined spreads for each security. Furthermore, both subsidiaries will pay accrued interest through the day preceding the settlement date. The repurchases reduce outstanding debt principal while requiring cash payments according to the announced tender terms. ExxonMobil shares fell $2.59 during the session, marking a 1.62% decline to $157.40. Earlier buying briefly lifted the stock toward $161.70 before sustained selling reversed those gains. Consequently, XOM finished the reported trading period near its intraday lows despite the company’s debt announcement. The debt repurchases follow ExxonMobil’s acquisition of Pioneer Natural Resources, which expanded its Permian Basin operations. That acquisition also brought Pioneer’s existing debt obligations into ExxonMobil’s broader corporate structure. The latest tender program addresses selected outstanding securities rather than the company’s entire debt portfolio. The announced results confirm full acceptance of valid tenders without exceeding the established $3 billion ceiling. Additionally, the final accepted amount leaves approximately $1.24 billion below the maximum authorized principal amount. XOM’s share decline accompanied the announcement, although the reported trading figures do not establish its underlying cause.
